analysis.one_liner: Restores community lending requirements for banks that the 1999 banking law weakened.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in a House Banking subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Weeks after Congress passed the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which let banks expand into securities and insurance, this bill would have tied that expansion back to a bank's community lending record. A bank holding company could only take on the new activities if all of its banks had a 'satisfactory' or better rating under the Community Reinvestment Act, which grades banks on how well they serve low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. It also would have repealed parts of the new law that reduced CRA exams for small banks, required public disclosure of CRA agreements, and ordered federal studies of the CRA.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, who rely on the Community Reinvestment Act to push banks to lend, open branches, and provide services in their communities rather than taking deposits and lending elsewhere.

how_it_helps.text: A bank holding company could expand into the new financial activities allowed by the 1999 law only if every depository institution it owns had a 'satisfactory' or better CRA rating, with a limited 12-month exclusion for newly acquired banks that submit an approved improvement plan.
The same CRA test would apply to national banks that want to control a financial subsidiary, closing a parallel path created by the 1999 law.
It repeals the graduated schedule that reduced CRA examinations for small banks, so small banks would be examined on meeting community credit needs on a regular basis again.

It repeals the requirement for public disclosure and annual reporting of CRA agreements between banks and community groups, along with mandated federal studies of the CRA, undoing several provisions added by the 1999 law.

analysis.who_pays: Large bank holding companies and financial conglomerates, which would have to keep satisfactory community lending ratings to use their new expansion powers, and small community banks, which would face more frequent CRA examinations and compliance work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks and small community banks

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 'sunshine' provision removes the only public disclosure of CRA agreements negotiated between banks and community groups, reducing transparency about how CRA money is pledged and spent.
Repealing the small-bank stretch-out restores regular CRA examinations for small banks, a real compliance cost for community banks that the 1999 law had deliberately reduced.

Conditioning expansion on CRA ratings could slow bank mergers and the entry of bank holding companies into securities and insurance, which supporters of the 1999 law argued would modernize financial services for customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is restoring a leverage point: banks that want the new expansion powers would have to keep serving their local communities. The costs are real but narrower — extra examination and paperwork burdens on small banks, and a loss of public disclosure of CRA agreements, which cuts against transparency even as it removes a paperwork burden banks disliked. The disclosure repeal was the most poorly designed piece; the rest is a targeted response to the community-lending provisions stripped out of the 1999 law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its financial institutions subcommittee on December 2, 1999, and never got a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters introduced the bill on November 18, 1999, with 16 original cosponsors, less than a week after the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act had cleared Congress.
It gathered 21 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 1 Independent, and was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services.
On December 2, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and financial conglomerates that had just won expanded powers under the 1999 law are better off, because nothing now conditions those powers on a satisfactory community lending record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks with new expansion powers

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CRA Restoration Act and recruited 16 original cosponsors within days of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's passage.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Clyburn, Conyers, Frank, Sanders (I), and Maloney.

against.name: Rep. Jim Leach
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill, referred it to a subcommittee on December 2, 1999, and never held a markup or advanced it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies and financial conglomerates
industries.note: The bill would condition their new power to enter securities and insurance on satisfactory community lending ratings. Banks had just obtained those powers without the CRA condition, and their gain came from a law that simultaneously trimmed CRA obligations.
They would regain the more frequent CRA examinations the 1999 law had reduced, a compliance cost. Unlike large conglomerates, they did not gain from the weakened CRA provisions being repealed.

industries.industry: Securities and insurance firms seeking bank affiliations
industries.note: Fewer bank holding companies would qualify to affiliate with them if expansion required satisfactory CRA ratings, slowing the financial consolidation the 1999 law enabled.
